## What are we trying to understand?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson tt-lesson"><p>Suppose we want to compare average scores on a hypothetical attention test. Our earlier lessons used a known population standard deviation of 10. In actual research, the population SD is often unknown; we estimate it from sample data. How does that change our inference? And what if we compare two different groups rather than the same people measured twice?</p><p>This optional lesson supports Weeks 9–10. All observations are synthetic examples.</p><div class="clt-overview"><p><strong>Learning goals</strong></p><ol><li>Explain why Student’s t distribution has heavier tails than the standard normal when degrees of freedom are small.</li><li>Choose a one-sample, independent-samples, or paired-samples t-test based on the research design.</li><li>Explain how the variability of paired differences affects standard error and inference.</li><li>Interpret a t-statistic, p-value, confidence interval, and statistical decision without equating significance with practical importance.</li></ol><p><strong>Before starting:</strong> Review sample SD, standard error, confidence intervals, and two-sided hypothesis tests.</p></div></div>
~~~

## Make a prediction and explore

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson tt-lesson" id="tt-lesson"><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="prediction"><legend>When variability is estimated from a small sample, how does the 95% t critical value compare with the standard normal critical value?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-prediction" value="smaller"> It is smaller.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-prediction" value="same"> It is exactly the same.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-prediction" value="wider"> It is larger, reflecting additional uncertainty.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check prediction</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><section class="clt-simulator" aria-labelledby="tt-distribution-title"><h2 id="tt-distribution-title">1. Compare Student’s t and the standard normal</h2><p class="clt-lead">Both distributions are centered at zero. The t distribution has heavier tails when degrees of freedom are small. Change degrees of freedom and alpha to explore how the critical values change.</p><div class="clt-controls"><div class="clt-control"><label for="tt-df">Degrees of freedom</label><select id="tt-df"><option value="3">3</option><option value="5" selected>5</option><option value="9">9</option><option value="19">19</option><option value="29">29</option><option value="99">99</option></select></div><div class="clt-control"><label for="tt-alpha">Significance level (α) — applies to both activities</label><select id="tt-alpha"><option value=".01">.01</option><option value=".05" selected>.05</option><option value=".10">.10</option></select></div></div><div class="tt-metrics"><div class="tt-metric"><span>Degrees of freedom</span><strong data-output="df">—</strong></div><div class="tt-metric"><span>Positive t critical value</span><strong data-output="critical">—</strong></div><div class="tt-metric"><span>Combined rejection-tail area</span><strong data-output="tail">—</strong></div></div><div class="tt-chart-wrap" data-chart="distribution"></div><div class="tt-legend"><span><i class="tt-key" aria-hidden="true"></i>Student’s t</span><span><i class="tt-key normal" aria-hidden="true"></i>Standard normal</span><span><i class="tt-key tail" aria-hidden="true"></i>t rejection regions</span></div><p class="clt-caption">The dashed vertical boundaries mark ± the t critical value. The two shaded tails together have probability α under the t model. At α = .05 the standard normal critical value is approximately 1.96. A one-sample t-test has n − 1 degrees of freedom; Welch’s test uses a different calculation. This distribution selector is independent of the sample design below.</p></section><section class="clt-simulator" aria-labelledby="tt-design-title"><h2 id="tt-design-title">2. Compare means using the appropriate design</h2><p class="clt-lead">Explore three hypothetical study designs, each testing a two-sided null hypothesis of zero mean difference. The numerical examples share the same marginal scores for comparison; they represent different hypothetical designs, not interchangeable analyses of one real study.</p><div class="clt-controls"><div class="clt-control"><label for="tt-method">Study design / statistical test</label><select id="tt-method"><option value="one">One sample vs reference (one-sample t)</option><option value="independent">Two independent groups (Welch t)</option><option value="paired" selected>Same students twice (paired t)</option></select></div><div data-pairing><div class="clt-control"><label for="tt-pattern">Hypothetical pairing pattern</label><select id="tt-pattern"><option value="aligned" selected>Similar before / after ranks</option><option value="reversed">Reversed ranks (different hypothetical pairs)</option></select></div></div></div><p data-output="design"></p><div class="clt-control"><label for="tt-delta">Difference between means (points): <output data-output="delta">3</output></label><input type="range" id="tt-delta" min="-6" max="8" step="1" value="3" aria-describedby="tt-delta-help"><span class="clt-help" id="tt-delta-help">Change the second set of scores by the same amount. The mean difference changes; its variability stays fixed within each pairing pattern.</span></div><div class="clt-action-row"><button class="clt-btn clt-secondary" type="button" data-action="reset">Restore starting settings</button></div><h3>Look at the observations</h3><div class="tt-chart-wrap" data-chart="data"></div><p class="clt-caption">The connecting lines appear only for paired data and represent individual students. Overlapping scores can share a location; the table gives every value. The paired-pattern control creates a different hypothetical dataset with identical marginal values; never rearrange real matched observations to obtain a preferred result.</p><details><summary>View all illustrative observations</summary><table class="tt-table"><caption>For paired data, each row is one student. For independent data, row positions have no matching meaning.</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Row</th><th scope="col">A / before</th><th scope="col">B / after</th><th scope="col">B − A (paired only)</th></tr></thead><tbody data-output="rows"></tbody></table></details><table class="clt-summary"><caption>Observed sample summaries</caption><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Mean A or fixed reference</th><td data-output="meanA">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Mean B / observed sample</th><td data-output="meanB">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Sample SD A</th><td data-output="sdA">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Sample SD B</th><td data-output="sdB">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Sample SD of paired differences</th><td data-output="sdDiff">—</td></tr></tbody></table><h3>Connect the difference to statistical evidence</h3><div class="tt-metrics"><div class="tt-metric"><span>Estimated difference</span><strong data-output="estimate">—</strong></div><div class="tt-metric"><span>Observed t statistic</span><strong data-output="t">—</strong></div><div class="tt-metric"><span>Two-sided p-value</span><strong data-output="p">—</strong></div></div><div class="tt-chart-wrap" data-chart="test"></div><div class="tt-legend"><span><i class="tt-key tail" aria-hidden="true"></i>At least as extreme as observed (both tails)</span></div><p class="clt-caption">The dot marks the observed t statistic. Both shaded tails represent the p-value under the selected null t distribution, not the rejection regions defined by alpha. The plot range expands for extreme statistics; probabilities use the entire distribution.</p><table class="clt-summary"><caption>Test results</caption><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Standard error of the estimated difference</th><td data-output="se">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Degrees of freedom</th><td data-output="testDf">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Confidence interval for the mean difference</th><td data-output="ci">—</td></tr></tbody></table><p>Confidence level: <strong><span data-output="ciLevel">—</span></strong>. <span data-output="formula">—</span></p><div class="tt-result" role="status" aria-live="polite"><p><strong><span data-output="decision">—</span></strong></p><p data-output="explanation"></p></div></section></div>

## Interpret what you find

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson tt-lesson"><ol><li>At α = .05 compare df = 3, 9, and 99 in Activity 1. What happens to the critical value and the two curves? Why is the small-sample t critical value larger than 1.96?</li><li>Set the mean difference to +3 and compare the one-sample and independent-samples designs. Write down their standard errors and degrees of freedom. Why are the tests not necessarily equally precise?</li><li>Use the paired design and compare similar ranks with reversed ranks. The two marginal means and SDs stay the same. What happens to the SD of the differences, the standard error, the p-value, and the confidence interval?</li><li>Set the difference to zero and then +3. Compare the p-value and confidence interval. Change alpha to .01 and explain the effect on the statistical decision and confidence interval, but not the p-value.</li></ol><p><strong>Think about it:</strong> What evidence about measurement quality, study design, practical importance, and assumptions would you want before drawing a conclusion about an intervention?</p></div>
~~~

## What are the t-tests telling us?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson tt-lesson"><p>When the population standard deviation is unknown, a t-test uses an estimated standard error. Student’s t distribution accounts for the additional uncertainty under the model. Smaller degrees of freedom give heavier tails and larger critical values for a given confidence level. As degrees of freedom increase, the t distribution approaches the standard normal.</p><div class="tt-formula"><strong>Common structure</strong><br>t = (estimated mean difference − hypothesized difference) / estimated standard error<br>Confidence interval = estimated difference ± critical t × estimated standard error<br>Two-sided p-value = probability of a t statistic at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null and model.</div><table class="tt-table"><caption>Choose by design, not by which test gives a smaller p-value</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Test</th><th scope="col">Estimated standard error</th><th scope="col">Key design requirement</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">One-sample</th><td>s / √n</td><td>Independent observations, fixed reference</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Independent (Welch)</th><td>√(sA²/nA + sB²/nB)</td><td>Two independent groups</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Paired</th><td>s of differences / √n</td><td>Meaningfully matched pairs, independent across pairs</td></tr></tbody></table><p><strong>Why pairing matters:</strong> The paired t-test is a one-sample t-test on within-person differences. When before and after scores tend to move together, differences can be less variable than the original scores. If pairing is weak or negative, this advantage may disappear. In the explorer, the hypothetical pairing pattern changes without changing the marginal scores; the estimated mean difference stays fixed but the variability of the differences changes.</p><p>The one-sample and paired t procedures are exact under independent normal observations or independent normal differences, respectively. Welch’s independent-samples test uses an approximate t reference distribution with estimated degrees of freedom and does not require equal population variances. With small samples, investigate skewness and influential outliers; larger samples can improve robustness, not repair dependence or selection bias. These deterministic examples illustrate calculation and design, not evidence that the assumptions hold.</p><p>Report the estimated difference, confidence interval, and p-value alongside context and limitations. A small p-value does not establish practical importance or causation, and failure to reject does not establish equality.</p></div>
~~~

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson tt-lesson" id="tt-knowledge-check"><p>These questions revisit the four learning goals. Your responses stay in your browser.</p><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="tails"><legend>1. How does the t distribution compare with the standard normal at small degrees of freedom?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-tails" value="light"> It has lighter tails.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-tails" value="heavy"> It has heavier tails.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-tails" value="same"> It is identical.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="choice"><legend>2. Ten students complete the same test before and after a program. Which method fits the design?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-choice" value="one"> One-sample t-test of only the after scores.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-choice" value="independent"> Independent-samples t-test.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-choice" value="paired"> Paired-samples t-test of the individual changes.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="precision"><legend>3. Which variability directly determines the paired t-test standard error?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-precision" value="difference"> Sample SD of the within-person differences.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-precision" value="after"> Sample SD of after scores alone.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-precision" value="total"> The sum of the two sample SDs.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="decision"><legend>4. A two-sided p-value of .12 exceeds α = .05. What can we conclude?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-decision" value="equal"> The two population means are proven equal.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-decision" value="insufficient"> There is insufficient evidence of a mean difference under the model.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="tt-q-decision" value="important"> The difference is necessarily unimportant.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><p><strong>Takeaway:</strong> Choose the test based on the design, quantify uncertainty using the correct estimated standard error, and interpret statistical evidence in context.</p><p>Textbook connection: OpenStax <em>Introductory Statistics 2e</em>, Chapters 8–10 (confidence intervals, one-sample hypothesis tests, and two-sample hypothesis tests).</p></div>
